```text
15	To verify that the Gini-based importance rankings in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features} are not an artifact of the impurity measure, we compute permutation importance (5-fold CV, 10 repeats) for all 9 atlas cells.
16	The top-2 features are stable across measures: \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in 9/9 cells under both Gini and permutation importance, and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 (vs.\ 7/9 for Gini, with the additional cell being OLMo top-$k$; the single SHAP exception is GPT-2~XL top-$k$, where \textsc{p75\_ppl} displaces \textsc{var\_surprisal} to rank 3).
17	The mean Spearman rank correlation between Gini and permutation importance vectors across all 9 cells is $\rho{=}0.76$ ($p{<}0.005$), indicating moderate-to-strong agreement; SHAP vs.\ permutation yields $\rho{\approx}0.83$.
18	Per-cell top-5 overlap between SHAP and permutation importance is 3--4 out of 5 features; the aggregated (mean-across-cells) top-5 sets are identical, confirming that the top features are robust to the choice of importance measure at the aggregate level while per-cell rankings exhibit model-dependent variation.
19	
20	\subsection{DCOL Iteration Details}
21	\label{app:dcol_iterations}
22	
23	Table~\ref{tab:dcol_iterations} summarizes all six DCOL iterations.
```

```json
    "newString": "\\paragraph{Controlled vs.\\ ecological setting.}\nAll experiments use Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generation (LoRA fine-tuning, 1--1.5B parameter models).\nWhile depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 59--82\\%, 3.4$\\times$ chance), a residual domain signal from seed-article stylistic differences exists (${\\sim}$2$\\times$ chance conditional on seed group; LOGO accuracy drops 8pp on average; Appendix~\\ref{app:domain_bias}).\nIn the most affected cell (Pythia top-$k$), individual LOGO folds drop to 22.9\\%, approaching chance.\nTransfer to mixed-domain corpora, instruction-tuned models, and larger scales (7B+) remains open.\nReal-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursion depths; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.",
    "originalFile": "\\section*{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}\nCross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.\nPer-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\\to}0.70$) but leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.\n\n\\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}\nDepth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\\% across all settings), inflating headline accuracy.\nCross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).\n\n\\paragraph{Controlled vs.\\ ecological setting.}\nAll experiments use Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generation (LoRA fine-tuning, 1--1.5B parameter models).\nTransfer to mixed-domain corpora, instruction-tuned models, and larger scales (7B+) remains open.\nWild-data calibration is probed only indirectly; ecological transfer is future work.\nReal-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursion depths; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.\n\n\\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}\nAdversarial paraphrasing \\cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}\nOur EDD definition (Eq.~\\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically---as observed in all our configurations.\nHowever, \\citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \\emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).\nOur cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.\nIn such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.\nThe choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.\n\n\\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}\nSurprisal-based features are computed relative to GPT-2 base (124M), introducing partial overlap when GPT-2~XL is held out, though GPT-2~XL holdout accuracy (67.6\\%) does not exceed the unrelated OLMo (69.2\\%).\nThe choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.\n\n\\paragraph{Additional caveats.}\nDetection features degrade under domain shift \\cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}; our depth features are likely susceptible.\n\\citet{falahati2026_curated} show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.\n\n\\section*{Ethics Statement}\n\nThis work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.\nNo human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.\nOur method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.",
```

     ```latex
     \section{Discussion and Conclusion}
     \label{sec:discussion}
     
     We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that 19 statistical features achieve 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$; cross-model 66.4\%, cross-strategy 59.1\%).
     
     \paragraph{Depth-aware data curation.}
     Predicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, enabling graded down-weighting of deeply recursive samples rather than binary discard \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
     However, our cross-strategy results (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) show that mid-depth classification degrades without knowledge of the decoding strategy, tempering expectations for uncontrolled settings.
     
     \paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment.}
     The residual gap after per-strategy normalization motivates a two-stage pipeline---strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification---leveraging the strategy-specific feature trajectories revealed by our atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).
     Combining depth estimation with watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} and model attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} could form a broader provenance toolkit.
     Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
     ```

extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.\n\n\\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}\nAdversarial paraphrasing \\cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}\nOur EDD definition (Eq.~\\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically---as observed in all our configurations.\nHowever, \\citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \\emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).\nOur cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.\nIn such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.\nThe choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.\n\n\\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}\nSurprisal-based features are computed relative to GPT-2 base (124M), introducing partial overlap when GPT-2~XL is held out, though GPT-2~XL holdout accuracy (67.6\\%) does not exceed the unrelated OLMo (69.2\\%).\nThe choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.\n\n\\paragraph{Additional caveats.}\nDetection features degrade under domain shift \\cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}; our depth features are likely susceptible.\n\\citet{falahati2026_curated} show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.\n\n\\section*{Ethics Statement}\n\nThis work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.\nNo human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.\nOur method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.",

```json
        "content": "\\section{Additional Results}\n\\label{app:additional}\n\n\\subsection{Top-$k$ Feature Trajectories}\n\\label{app:topk_trajectories}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:feature_trajectory} in the main text shows feature trajectories for nucleus ($p{=}0.95$) and temperature ($\\tau{=}0.9$) sampling.\nTop-$k$ ($k{=}50$) trajectories follow the same monotonically decreasing trend for all features but with compressed inter-depth spacing, consistent with the signal attenuation effect discussed in \\S\\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}.\nConcretely, the d0$\\to$d1 drop in \\textsc{p90\\_ppl} under top-$k$ is 78\\% (vs.\\ 87\\% for nucleus), and the d2$\\to$d3 reduction is 31\\% (vs.\\ 39\\% for nucleus).\nDespite the magnitude reduction, feature rank ordering across depths is preserved, which explains why ordinal classifiers maintain directionality even under top-$k$ conditions.\n\n\\subsection{Permutation Importance}\n\\label{app:permutation}\n\nTo verify that the Gini-based importance rankings in \\S\\ref{sec:atlas:features} are not an artifact of the impurity measure, we compute permutation importance (5-fold CV, 10 repeats) for all 9 atlas cells.\nThe top-2 features are stable across measures: \\textsc{p90\\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in 9/9 cells under both Gini and permutation importance, and \\textsc{var\\_surprisal} in 8/9 (vs.\\ 7/9 for Gini, with the additional cell being OLMo top-$k$; the single SHAP exception is GPT-2~XL top-$k$, where \\textsc{p75\\_ppl} displaces \\textsc{var\\_surprisal} to rank 3).\nKendall's $W{=}0.90$ across all three methods (Gini, permutation, SHAP) indicates strong concordance ($p{<}0.005$).\nPairwise Spearman correlations are: SHAP--Gini $\\rho{=}0.93$, SHAP--permutation $\\rho{=}0.84$, Gini--permutation $\\rho{=}0.76$.\nPer-cell top-5 overlap between SHAP and permutation importance is 3--4 out of 5 features; the aggregated (mean-across-cells) top-5 sets are identical, confirming that the top features are robust to the choice of importance measure at the aggregate level while per-cell rankings exhibit model-dependent variation.\n\n\\subsection{DCOL Iteration Details}\n\\label{app:dcol_iterations}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:dcol_iterations} summarizes all six DCOL iterations.\nDeBERTa-v3-large exhibited systematic numerical instability across five configurations; RoBERTa-large resolved stability but could not close the accuracy gap with feature-based methods.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{DCOL iteration summary. All experiments use Pythia-1.4B nucleus data. RF baseline: 78.2\\%.}\n\\label{tab:dcol_iterations}\n\\begin{tabular}{llll}\n\\toprule\nVer. & Backbone & Config & Outcome \\\\\n\\midrule\nv1 & DeBERTa-large & Full FT, margin\\_lr$\\,{=}\\,10^{-3}$ & Embed.\\ collapse (acc 31.5\\%) \\\\\nv2 & DeBERTa-large & Full FT, margin\\_lr$\\,{=}\\,10^{-4}$ & OOM (GPU contention) \\\\\nv3 & DeBERTa-large & Full FT, margin\\_lr$\\,{=}\\,10^{-4}$ & Forgetting $+$ OOM \\\\\nv4 & DeBERTa-large & LoRA $r{=}16$, m\\_lr$\\,{=}\\,10^{-3}$ & Embed.\\ collapse (v1 repeat) \\\\\nv5 & DeBERTa-large & LoRA $r{=}16$, m\\_lr$\\,{=}\\,10^{-4}$ & NaN gradient explosion \\\\\nv6 & RoBERTa-large & Full FT, grad clip 1.0 & Stable; acc 64.5\\% ($-$13.7pp) \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\subsection{Feature Overlap Analysis}\n\\label{app:feature_overlap}\n\nWe probe whether end-to-end PLM representations capture the same depth signals as our statistical features.\nDeBERTa attention importance and RF permutation importance exhibit a significant negative correlation (Spearman $\\rho{=}{-}0.484$, $p{=}0.036$; top-5 Jaccard overlap$\\,{=}\\,0$).\nPLM representations excel at surface lexical features (TTR: $R^2{=}0.85$, repeated bigrams) but fail to capture perplexity distribution statistics---\\textsc{var\\_surprisal} and \\textsc{p90\\_ppl} yield negative $R^2$ under linear probing.\nThis confirms that the 19pp accuracy gap between feature-based and end-to-end methods (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:e2e}) stems from complementary---not redundant---representations: PLMs capture lexical patterns while the statistical features capture distributional tail properties that constitute the dominant depth markers.\n\n\\subsection{Domain Bias Analysis}\n\\label{app:domain_bias}\n\nTo assess whether the classifier exploits depth-related features or memorizes stylistic cues from individual seed articles, we conduct a leave-one-group-out (LOGO) evaluation where each fold holds out all passages derived from a single Wikipedia seed article.\nAcross all 9 atlas cells, 5-fold CV accuracy ranges from 59\\% to 82\\% (3.4$\\times$ chance), confirming that depth signal is the dominant classification factor.\nHowever, a residual domain signal exists: conditional on seed group, accuracy reaches 28--33\\% (${\\sim}$2$\\times$ chance for the 4-class task), indicating that stylistic differences across seed articles contribute a secondary signal.\nLOGO accuracy drops 8pp on average relative to random-split CV, with substantial variance across cells.\nIn the most affected configuration (Pythia-1.4B, top-$k$), individual LOGO folds drop as low as 22.9\\%---approaching the 33.3\\% chance level for d1--d3 classification---suggesting that in specific model--strategy combinations, the seed-article effect can nearly eliminate the depth signal for a held-out article group.\nThese results motivate future work on domain-robust features and cross-corpus evaluation.\n",
```

```json
        "content": "\\section{Discussion and Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nWe formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that 19 statistical features achieve 70--85\\% four-class accuracy ($\\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$; cross-model 66.4\\%, cross-strategy 59.1\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Depth-aware data curation.}\nPredicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, enabling graded down-weighting of deeply recursive samples rather than binary discard \\cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.\nHowever, our cross-strategy results (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) show that mid-depth classification degrades without knowledge of the decoding strategy, tempering expectations for uncontrolled settings.\n\n\\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment.}\nThe residual gap after per-strategy normalization motivates a two-stage pipeline---strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification---leveraging the strategy-specific feature trajectories revealed by our atlas (\\S\\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).\nCombining depth estimation with watermarking \\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} and model attribution \\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} could form a broader provenance toolkit.\nCode and data will be released upon acceptance.\n",
        "numLines": 14,
        "startLine": 1,
        "totalLines": 14
      }
    },
```

```json
      "file": {
        "filePath": "/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0513_2/projects/recursive_gen_depth_est/docs/paper/abstract.tex",
        "content": "\\begin{abstract}\nAs large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\\to$data$\\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.\nWe formalize \\emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.\nFrom each passage we extract 19 statistical features---perplexity percentiles, surprisal moments, and lexical diversity measures---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).\nA Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\\%; 58.8--82.6\\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \\times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively).\nOur \\emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \\emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.\nCross-model transfer reaches 66.4\\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.\n\\end{abstract}",
        "numLines": 8,
        "startLine": 1,
        "totalLines": 8
      }
    },
    "displayPath": "../../../docs/paper/abstract.tex"
  },
```

```json
        "content": "\\section{Generalization and Robustness}\n\\label{sec:generalization}\n\nWe test whether the atlas results (69.6--85.4\\%) reflect genuine statistical regularities or training artifacts, evaluating four axes: classifier choice (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:baselines}), cross-model transfer (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossmodel}), cross-strategy transfer (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}), and end-to-end learning (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:e2e}).\n\n\\subsection{Baseline Comparison}\n\\label{sec:gen:baselines}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:baselines} compares classification methods on the Pythia-1.4B nucleus setting.\nThree feature-based methods---Random Forest (RF), CORAL ordinal regression \\cite{coral2020}, and DivEye \\cite{diveye2026}---all operate on the same 19 statistical features and achieve statistically indistinguishable accuracy (78.1--78.2\\%; pairwise bootstrap $p>0.05$ after Bonferroni correction, 95\\% CI within $\\pm$1.1pp).\nThese three significantly outperform CE-MLP ($p<0.001$, $+$3.8pp), which in turn trails logistic regression by $\\sim$0.1pp.\nSingle-feature regression on mean perplexity performs at chance (25.1\\%), confirming that depth estimation requires the multi-dimensional feature representation defined in \\S\\ref{sec:method}.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Comparison of classification methods on Pythia-1.4B nucleus. RF, CORAL, and DivEye use the same 19 statistical features and are statistically indistinguishable (bootstrap $p>0.05$, Bonferroni-corrected). Chance = 25\\%. 5-fold CV std: 0.2--0.9pp across all methods.}\n\\label{tab:baselines}\n\\begin{tabular}{lc}\n\\toprule\nMethod & 4-class Acc (\\%) \\\\\n\\midrule\nRF (19 features) & 78.2 \\\\\nCORAL & 78.1 \\\\\nDivEye & 78.2 \\\\\nCE-MLP & 74.9 \\\\\nLR & 75.0 \\\\\nDeepSeek V3.2 (zero-shot)\\footnotemark & 36.2 \\\\\nppl-regression (single feature) & 25.1 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\footnotetext{Evaluated on 500 samples (125 per class) from the Pythia-1.4B nucleus cell only, due to API cost; 95\\% CI: $[32.0\\%, 40.4\\%]$. All other methods use the full 20{,}000-sample set.}\n\\end{table}\n\nThat three structurally different classifiers achieve identical performance confirms that the discriminative signal resides in the 19 features, not the classifier architecture; a zero-shot LLM baseline (DeepSeek V3.2) reaches only 36.2\\%.\nFigure~\\ref{fig:confusion_matrix} shows d0 is near-perfectly identified in both settings; errors concentrate at the d2/d3 boundary in-distribution and spread across d1--d3 under cross-model transfer.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/fig_confusion_matrix.pdf}\n\\caption{Confusion matrices for the best in-distribution setting (GPT-2 XL, temp $\\tau{=}0.9$, 85.4\\%) and the best cross-model leave-one-out transfer (OLMo holdout, 69.2\\%). d0 recall exceeds 99\\% in both; errors spread across the d1--d3 range under transfer.}\n\\label{fig:confusion_matrix}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}\n\\label{sec:gen:crossmodel}\n\nWe perform leave-one-model-family-out evaluation: train on two families (nucleus only), test on the held-out third (Table~\\ref{tab:cross_model}).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Cross-model transfer (leave-one-out, nucleus only). Train on 2 model families, test on held-out 3rd. Chance = 25\\%. d0 recall $>$98\\% inflates headline accuracy; d1--d3 balanced accuracy averages 55.5\\%.}\n\\label{tab:cross_model}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccccc}\n\\toprule\nHoldout & Acc & d0 & d1 & d2 & d3 \\\\\n & (\\%) & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. \\\\\n\\midrule\nPythia & 62.4 & 100.0 & 49.3 & 26.8 & 73.6 \\\\\nOLMo & \\textbf{69.2} & 99.3 & 75.5 & 43.3 & 58.8 \\\\\nGPT-2 XL & 67.6 & 98.5 & 74.7 & 52.6 & 44.5 \\\\\n\\midrule\nMean & 66.4 & 99.3 & 66.5 & 40.9 & 59.0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nMean transfer accuracy reaches 66.4\\% (2.7$\\times$ chance); d0 recall ($>$98\\%) inflates the headline while d2 drops to 26.8\\% (Pythia holdout).\nExcluding d0, the d1--d3 balanced accuracy averages 55.5\\% across holdout conditions (Pythia 49.9\\%, OLMo 59.2\\%, GPT-2~XL 57.3\\%; chance = 33\\%).\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Strategy Transfer}\n\\label{sec:gen:crossstrategy}\n\nWe train on two decoding strategies and test on the held-out third (Table~\\ref{tab:cross_strategy}).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Cross-strategy transfer (leave-one-out). Train on 2 strategies, test on held-out 3rd. Chance = 25\\%. d0 recall $\\geq$89.5\\% inflates headline accuracy.}\n\\label{tab:cross_strategy}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\nHoldout & Pythia & OLMo & GPT-2 XL \\\\\n & Acc (\\%) & Acc (\\%) & Acc (\\%) \\\\\n\\midrule\nnucleus & \\textbf{69.4} & \\textbf{65.4} & \\textbf{59.9} \\\\\ntemp ($\\tau{=}0.9$) & 62.8 & 58.2 & 56.1 \\\\\ntop-$k$ ($k{=}50$) & 51.5 & 54.9 & 53.6 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nMean cross-strategy accuracy (59.1\\%) falls 7pp below cross-model transfer (66.4\\%), indicating that strategy-induced shifts pose a greater challenge than architectural differences.\nAs with cross-model transfer, d0 recall remains high ($\\geq$89.5\\%), inflating headline accuracy; excluding d0, d1--d3 accuracy drops further (45.9\\%; chance = 33\\%).\nd2 recall ranges from 3.7\\% to 19\\%, confirming mid-chain depths as the primary confusion locus.\n\n\\paragraph{Temperature-induced boundary inversion.}\nTraining on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature inverts the d1/d2 boundary (d1v2 AUC $<$ 0.5; \\S\\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).\nPer-strategy z-score normalization partially recovers the boundary but leaves a residual gap to within-strategy performance (per-model details in Limitations).\n\n\\subsection{End-to-End Learning}\n\\label{sec:gen:e2e}\n\nDeBERTa-v3-base \\cite{he2021_deberta_v3} and RoBERTa-base \\cite{liu2019_roberta} finetuned end-to-end both converge to ${\\sim}$59\\% (19pp below RF 78.2\\%; 1.2pp inter-backbone gap rules out architecture bias).\nLinear probing yields negative $R^2$ for \\textsc{var\\_surprisal} and \\textsc{p90\\_ppl} from DeBERTa hidden states (Appendix~\\ref{app:feature_overlap}), yet SHAP attributes 88.8\\% of RF's contribution to perplexity/surprisal features.\nDCOL \\cite{cloc2025} reached 64.5\\% (Appendix~\\ref{app:dcol_iterations}); all end-to-end approaches (58--65\\%) underperform feature-based methods.",
```

```text
1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Definition}
5	\label{sec:method:problem}
6	
7	Let $f_\theta$ denote a language model and $\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.
8	We define a \emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\mathcal{D}_0, \mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.
9	Depth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.
10	
11	Given a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$.
12	This is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.
13	
14	\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}
15	\label{sec:method:benchmark}
16	
17	We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.
18	
19	\paragraph{Model families.}
20	We select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).
21	Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
24	Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
25	These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.
26	
27	\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
28	The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).
29	For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.
30	
31	\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
32	Starting from a Wikipedia subset as seed text ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each generation cycle proceeds in three steps: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} with rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, for 3 epochs; (2)~generation of 5{,}000 passages (max 512 tokens) under the specified decoding strategy; (3)~the generated corpus becomes $\mathcal{D}_k$ and serves as training data for the next cycle.
33	Each generation cycle samples unconditionally from the BOS token; there is no per-passage lineage across depths, ensuring that cross-validation splits do not introduce information leakage.
34	LoRA targets are architecture-specific: \texttt{query\_key\_value} for Pythia (GPT-NeoX), \texttt{q\_proj}/\texttt{k\_proj}/\texttt{v\_proj} for OLMo, and \texttt{c\_attn}/\texttt{c\_proj} for GPT-2~XL.
35	We adopt commonly used LoRA hyperparameters ($r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout$\,{=}\,0.05$) following \citet{hu2022lora}, applied uniformly across all models.
36	
37	\paragraph{Reference model.}
38	All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) are computed using a fixed reference model---GPT-2 base (124M)---that is independent of the three generation models.
39	The reference model computes per-token perplexity for each passage, providing a consistent measurement frame across model families.
40	In cross-model leave-one-out evaluation (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), the reference model remains fixed even when GPT-2~XL is held out; the partial architectural overlap this introduces is discussed in Limitations.
41	
42	\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
43	\label{sec:method:features}
44	
45	We extract a 19-dimensional feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$.
46	The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).
47	
48	\begin{table}[t]
49	\centering
50	\small
51	\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).}
52	\label{tab:features}
53	\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
54	\toprule
55	Category & Features & $n$ \\
56	\midrule
57	Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
58	statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
59	\addlinespace
60	Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
61	statistics & & \\
62	\addlinespace
63	Lexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\
64	diversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\
65	\addlinespace
66	Repetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\
67	\bottomrule
68	\end{tabular}
69	\end{table}
70	
71	\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the location, spread, and shape of the per-token perplexity distribution via its mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, and five percentile quantiles (p10--p90).
72	The tail quantiles (p75, p90) prove especially informative: recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail, making these features monotonically decreasing with depth (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
73	
74	\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features) operate on $-\log p(\text{token})$ and include mean surprisal, surprisal variance, and the entropy of the surprisal distribution.
75	While correlated with perplexity features, surprisal variance captures second-order structure---the variability of token predictability---that is not redundant with perplexity moments.
76	
77	\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features) measures vocabulary usage through type--token ratio, hapax ratio (fraction of tokens appearing exactly once), and bigram/trigram entropy.
78	
79	\emph{Repetition} (3 features) quantifies the fraction of repeated $n$-grams for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$, capturing the increased self-repetition characteristic of recursive generation.
80	
81	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
82	\label{sec:method:edd}
83	
84	Aggregate classification accuracy over $K{+}1$ classes obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depths.
85	We introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD), a scalar metric that summarizes how far into a recursive chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.
86	
87	For each adjacent depth pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we train a dedicated binary Random Forest (500 trees; increased from 200 in the multi-class setting to ensure convergence on the smaller per-pair samples) and compute the one-vs-one AUC.
88	Given a threshold $T$, we define:
89	\begin{equation}
90	\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \bigl\{ d^*{+}1 : \forall\, d' \leq d^*,\; \mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \geq T \bigr\}
91	\label{eq:edd}
92	\end{equation}
93	where $d^* \in \{0, 1, \dots, K{-}1\}$.\footnote{Our AUC profiles are monotonically decreasing, so the $\forall$ and pointwise $\max\{d^*{+}1 : \mathrm{AUC}(d^*,d^*{+}1) \geq T\}$ formulations coincide; the $\forall$ version is preferred as it guarantees a contiguous discriminable range (see Limitations).}
94	The default threshold is $T{=}0.75$; we report sensitivity analyses at $T \in \{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\}$ in \S\ref{sec:atlas}.
95	Crucially, each AUC is obtained from an independent binary pairwise classifier (5-fold stratified CV) rather than extracted from a single multi-class model, avoiding decision boundary dilution (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
96	
97	EDD captures a natural question: \emph{how deep into the recursive chain can we reliably distinguish successive generations?}
98	A high EDD indicates that the statistical fingerprints retain discriminative power across many recursion steps; a low EDD signals rapid convergence to an indistinguishable regime.
99	
100	\paragraph{Classifiers.}
101	Our primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold stratified cross-validation).
102	We compare against CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral2020}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, a 2-layer cross-entropy MLP, logistic regression, and a single-feature baseline using mean perplexity alone; results appear in \S\ref{sec:generalization}.
```

entropy.\n\n\\emph{Repetition} (3 features) quantifies the fraction of repeated $n$-grams for $n \\in \\{2, 3, 4\\}$, capturing the increased self-repetition characteristic of recursive generation.\n\n\\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}\n\\label{sec:method:edd}\n\nAggregate classification accuracy over $K{+}1$ classes obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depths.\nWe introduce the \\emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD), a scalar metric that summarizes how far into a recursive chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.\n\nFor each adjacent depth pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we train a dedicated binary Random Forest (500 trees; increased from 200 in the multi-class setting to ensure convergence on the smaller per-pair samples) and compute the one-vs-one AUC.\nGiven a threshold $T$, we define:\n\\begin{equation}\n\\mathrm{EDD}_T = \\max \\bigl\\{ d^*{+}1 : \\forall\\, d' \\leq d^*,\\; \\mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \\geq T \\bigr\\}\n\\label{eq:edd}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d^* \\in \\{0, 1, \\dots, K{-}1\\}$.\\footnote{Our AUC profiles are monotonically decreasing, so the $\\forall$ and pointwise $\\max\\{d^*{+}1 : \\mathrm{AUC}(d^*,d^*{+}1) \\geq T\\}$ formulations coincide; the $\\forall$ version is preferred as it guarantees a contiguous discriminable range (see Limitations).}\nThe default threshold is $T{=}0.75$; we report sensitivity analyses at $T \\in \\{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\\}$ in \\S\\ref{sec:atlas}.\nCrucially, each AUC is obtained from an independent binary pairwise classifier (5-fold stratified CV) rather than extracted from a single multi-class model, avoiding decision boundary dilution (\\S\\ref{sec:atlas}).\n\nEDD captures a natural question: \\emph{how deep into the recursive chain can we reliably distinguish successive generations?}\nA high EDD indicates that the statistical fingerprints retain discriminative power across many recursion steps; a low EDD signals rapid convergence to an indistinguishable regime.\n\n\\paragraph{Classifiers.}\nOur primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold stratified cross-validation).\nWe compare against CORAL ordinal regression \\cite{coral2020}, DivEye \\cite{diveye2026}, a 2-layer cross-entropy MLP, logistic regression, and a single-feature baseline using mean perplexity alone; results appear in \\S\\ref{sec:generalization}.",

```text
1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
5	As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
6	This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
7	
8	Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
9	Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
10	Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
11	The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
12	No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.
13	
14	Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are consistent across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
15	Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.
16	
17	We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
18	Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
19	To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
20	The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.
21	
22	Our contributions are:
23	
24	\begin{itemize}
25	    \item \textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.
26	
27	    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 8/9, with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. The extended Pythia nucleus pipeline (d0--d5) yields $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$, establishing that depth discrimination persists through four recursive steps before falling below threshold.
28	
29	    \item \textbf{Generalization analysis.} Cross-model leave-one-out transfer achieves 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\% (chance = 25\%). We decompose a temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion into a scale component---partially correctable by per-strategy normalization---and a residual structural component that simple normalization cannot resolve.
30	
31	    \item \textbf{End-to-end learning.} Both DeBERTa-v3-base (58.3\%) and RoBERTa-base (59.5\%) achieve ${\sim}$59\% via end-to-end finetuning---19pp below feature-based classifiers (78.2\%)---with the architecture-invariant gap ruling out model selection bias. Linear probing confirms that PLM representations cannot recover perplexity tail features (negative $R^2$), while SHAP analysis shows these features account for 88.8\% of RF's contribution.
32	\end{itemize}
```

```json
      "content": "\\section{Introduction}\n\\label{sec:intro}\n\nThe text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.\nAs synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \\cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.\nThis model$\\to$data$\\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \\cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.\n\nExisting tools address adjacent but distinct problems.\nBinary detectors such as Binoculars \\cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \\cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \\cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \\geq 1$ into a single category.\nWatermarking \\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.\nThe model collapse literature \\cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \\citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.\nNo existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.\n\nOur key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are consistent across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.\nSpecifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\\textsc{p90\\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\\textsc{var\\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.\n\nWe formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.\nGiven a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).\nTo systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \\emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \\times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.\nThe atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \\emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.\n\nOur contributions are:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item \\textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \\times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \\textsc{p90\\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells and \\textsc{var\\_surprisal} in 8/9, with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. Linear probing confirms that PLM representations cannot recover perplexity tail features (negative $R^2$), while SHAP analysis shows these features account for 88.8\\% of RF's contribution.\n\\end{itemize}",
```

```text
1	\begin{abstract}
2	As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
3	We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
4	From each passage we extract 19 statistical features---perplexity percentiles, surprisal moments, and lexical diversity measures---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
5	A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; 58.8--82.6\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively).
6	Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
7	Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.
8	\end{abstract}
```

```text
1	\section{The Depth Degradation Atlas}
2	\label{sec:atlas}
3	
4	We present the Depth Degradation Atlas: a systematic empirical map of how statistical fingerprints evolve across recursive generation depths, models, and decoding strategies.
5	The atlas spans $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells evaluated at depths $d \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, with depth extensions to $d{=}5$ for cross-model EDD validation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).
6	
7	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
8	\subsection{In-Distribution Performance}
9	\label{sec:atlas:id}
10	
11	Table~\ref{tab:main_matrix} reports four-class Random Forest accuracy (5-fold CV, 200 trees) across all nine cells.
12	Accuracy ranges from 69.6\% (Pythia, top-$k$) to 85.4\% (GPT-2~XL, temperature), all exceeding the 25\% chance baseline by a wide margin.
13	Two axis effects emerge.
14	GPT-2~XL achieves the highest accuracy under every strategy (76.6--85.4\%), followed by OLMo (74.2--82.0\%) and Pythia (69.6--78.2\%).
15	Top-$k$ sampling yields the lowest accuracy in every model.
16	The mean within-model strategy gap is 8.4~pp, comparable to the 7.1~pp mean within-strategy model gap---decoding strategy and model family contribute roughly equally to performance variance.

35	\subsection{Feature Universality}
36	\label{sec:atlas:features}
37	
38	Despite the 15.8~pp accuracy spread across cells, a small feature family dominates in every setting.
39	The 90th-percentile perplexity (\texttt{p90\_ppl}) ranks top-2 by Gini importance in all 9 cells; surprisal variance (\texttt{var\_surprisal}) in 7/9 (8/9 under SHAP; Appendix~\ref{app:permutation}).
40	Table~\ref{tab:feature_importance} shows the full per-cell ranking.
41	
42	Cross-model feature-rank Spearman correlation averages $\bar{\rho} = 0.868$ (range $[0.619, 0.954]$): models agree on which features carry depth information even when they differ in absolute accuracy.
43	Among strategies, top-$k$ yields the highest cross-model rank correlation ($\rho = 0.811$)---the deterministic vocabulary truncation imposes a more uniform feature landscape across architectures, at the cost of weaker overall signal (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).
44	
45	Percentile-based features outperform their moment-based counterparts.
46	Token-level perplexity distributions are heavy-tailed: individual outlier passages can dominate the arithmetic mean of their depth class, whereas \texttt{p90\_ppl} is robust to such extremes while still capturing the tail erosion that signals recursive depth.
47	
48	The feature hierarchy also shifts with depth.
49	At shallow boundaries (d1 vs.\ d2), \texttt{var\_surprisal} dominates importance; at deeper boundaries (d3 vs.\ d4, d4 vs.\ d5), tail perplexity statistics (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{kurtosis\_ppl}) take over.
50	This transition aligns with model-collapse dynamics~\cite{shumailov2024_nature}: early recursion narrows the surprisal distribution (captured by its variance), while later steps erode the perplexity tail (captured by upper quantiles and kurtosis).

75	\subsection{Monotonicity and Inter-Depth Distances}
76	\label{sec:atlas:monotonicity}
77	
78	Depth features exhibit strong monotonic trends.

80	Two complementary signal groups drive this structure.
81	Perplexity tail statistics (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{mean\_surprisal}) decrease monotonically with depth ($\rho = -1.0$ across cell-level medians), reflecting the narrowing of the token-predictability distribution under recursive finetuning.
82	Repetition features (\texttt{rep\_2gram}, \texttt{rep\_3gram}, \texttt{rep\_4gram}) increase monotonically, capturing the growing self-repetition that accompanies distribution collapse.
83	
84	Inter-depth distances are non-uniform.

86	The $d{=}0 \to d{=}1$ gap reflects the qualitative jump from human-written to machine-generated text; subsequent recursion steps produce progressively smaller distributional shifts.
87	This non-uniformity has practical implications: distinguishing real from first-generation synthetic text is near-trivial, but separating adjacent deep generations requires increasingly sensitive features---precisely the tail statistics identified in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}.

97	\subsection{EDD Analysis}
98	\label{sec:atlas:edd}
99	
100	We extend the benchmark to depth $d{=}5$ for all three models under nucleus sampling.
101	Each model's depth-3 LoRA checkpoint is used to finetune and generate depth-4 data, and the process repeats for depth~5; feature extraction uses the same reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
102	We train dedicated binary RF classifiers (500 trees) for each adjacent pair, as defined in Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}.
103	
104	\paragraph{AUC decay profile.}
105	Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} plots the binary pairwise AUC decay curves.
106	For Pythia-1.4B (nucleus), AUC decays monotonically: d0-vs-d1 $= 0.999$, d1-vs-d2 $= 0.925$, d2-vs-d3 $= 0.823$, d3-vs-d4 $= 0.784$, d4-vs-d5 $= 0.683$.
107	The steepest drop occurs between the d1-vs-d2 and d2-vs-d3 pairs; the curve then flattens as the system approaches an indistinguishable regime gradually rather than crossing a sharp boundary.
108	
109	\paragraph{Cross-model convergence at depth 4--5.}
110	All three models exhibit a consistent profile at the deep boundaries.
111	The d3-vs-d4 AUC clusters near the $T{=}0.75$ threshold: Pythia $0.784$ (bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.765, 0.802]$, $p = 0.001$), OLMo $0.765$ ($[0.744, 0.785]$, $p = 0.091$), GPT-2~XL $0.750$ ($[0.728, 0.771]$, $p = 0.505$), where $p$ denotes the one-tailed bootstrap probability under $H_0\!: \mathrm{AUC} \leq 0.75$ (1{,}000 iterations).
112	Only Pythia achieves significance at conventional levels; OLMo is marginal and GPT-2~XL falls on the threshold despite its higher in-distribution accuracy.
113	The d4-vs-d5 AUC falls uniformly below 0.70 across all three models (Pythia $0.683$, OLMo $0.684$, GPT-2~XL $0.681$), confirming a model-independent signal saturation point at depth~5.
114	
115	This pattern---directional consistency across models with graded statistical strength---supports interpreting the d3--d4 region as a \emph{transition zone} rather than a binary boundary.
116	The continuous AUC decay curve provides a more informative characterization of depth discriminability than any single $\mathrm{EDD}_T$ value.
117	
118	\paragraph{EDD threshold sensitivity.}
119	Table~\ref{tab:edd_sensitivity} reports $\mathrm{EDD}_T$ across the primary 9-cell benchmark (depths 0--3) at four threshold values.
120	At $T{=}0.65$, all 9 cells achieve $\mathrm{EDD} = 3$; at $T{=}0.75$, 7 of 9 cells maintain $\mathrm{EDD} \geq 3$; at $T{=}0.80$, the count drops to 5 of 9.

144	\paragraph{Decision boundary dilution.}
145	\label{sec:atlas:edd:dilution}
146	EDD's binary-pair design is motivated by \emph{decision boundary dilution}: when a multi-class classifier must simultaneously separate $K$ depths, its decision boundaries are shared across all $\binom{K}{2}$ class pairs, diluting the capacity allocated to any single adjacent pair.
147	Concretely, in the Pythia nucleus setting, the d2\,vs.\,d3 pairwise AUC degrades from 0.804 in a 4-class pipeline to 0.689 in a 6-class pipeline---a 14.3\% relative decline---despite identical underlying data.
148	Mean classification accuracy likewise drops from 99.5\% (binary) to 78.3\% (4-class) to 62.9\% (6-class).
149	Because the pairwise signal between depths $d$ and $d{+}1$ does not change when unrelated depths are added, this degradation is entirely attributable to boundary dilution, not signal loss.
150	Binary pairwise classifiers eliminate this confound, isolating the true adjacent-pair discriminability that EDD is designed to measure.
151	
152	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
153	\subsection{Strategy-Dependent Trajectories}
154	\label{sec:atlas:strategy}
155	
156	The three decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories that resist reduction to a binary taxonomy.
157	
158	\paragraph{Nucleus ($p{=}0.95$): stable baseline.}
159	Nucleus sampling produces the most consistent accuracy across models (78.2--83.3\%), with moderate AUC decay and no anomalous pairwise boundaries.
160	It serves as the reference trajectory against which temperature and top-$k$ effects are measured.
161	
162	\paragraph{Temperature ($\tau{=}0.9$): signal enhancement with boundary reversal.}
163	Temperature sampling yields the highest accuracy in 2 of 3 models (GPT-2~XL $85.4\%$, OLMo $82.0\%$) and the second-highest in Pythia ($76.3\%$).
164	Unlike nucleus and top-$k$, which truncate the vocabulary, temperature uniformly scales logits, redistributing probability mass across all tokens.
165	This accelerates convergence to an attractor distribution during recursive finetuning~\cite{shumailov2024_nature}, amplifying the statistical fingerprint at each depth step.
166	The acceleration manifests as a systematic depth shift: temperature depth-$N$ features approximate nucleus/top-$k$ depth-$(N{+}1)$ features.
167	For GPT-2~XL, temperature depth-1 \texttt{p90\_ppl} median is 92.2, falling within the nucleus/top-$k$ depth-2 range of 65--92.
168	
169	This depth shift creates a boundary reversal risk in cross-strategy transfer (\S\ref{sec:generalization}): a classifier trained on nucleus and top-$k$ data systematically overpredicts depth for temperature-generated text, because temperature depth-1 features overlap with nucleus/top-$k$ depth-2 features.
170	
171	\paragraph{Top-$k$ ($k{=}50$): signal attenuation, direction preserved.}
172	Top-$k$ sampling produces the lowest accuracy in every model (69.6--76.6\%), with a mean 8.4~pp gap from the strongest strategy.
173	Hard vocabulary truncation removes low-probability tokens that carry depth-discriminative information, attenuating the overall signal.
174	The \emph{direction} of feature evolution, however, is preserved: perplexity statistics still decrease monotonically with depth, and feature importance rankings maintain the highest cross-model correlation ($\rho = 0.811$).
175	Top-$k$ compresses the depth signal without distorting it.
176	
177	\paragraph{Strategy vs.\ model effect.}
178	The strategy effect (8.4~pp range) exceeds the model effect (7.1~pp range) across the atlas, indicating that deployment-time knowledge of the decoding strategy is at least as important as knowledge of the generator model for accurate depth estimation.
179
```

```text
1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
5	\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursively training language models on their own outputs erodes distributional tails, eventually collapsing the output distribution to a narrow mode.
6	\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this phenomenon through scaling laws that distinguish tail \emph{narrowing} (reduced variance) from tail \emph{cutting} (lost support), showing both accelerate with generation depth; \citet{dohmatob2024_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and \citet{dohmatob2024_demystified} analyze the regression case.
7	The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this analysis to self-consuming generative models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff as synthetic data accumulates across generations.
8	Mitigation strategies include retaining real data \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} and filtering synthetic samples via detection \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
9	Recent work identifies non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, fixed-point convergence \cite{marchi2024_heat_death}, contamination bounds \cite{wang2026_contamination}, curated pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
10	These works characterize degradation patterns but assume the generation depth is known a priori; our work addresses the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.
11	
12	\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
13	DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature---the tendency of model-generated text to occupy local maxima of the log-probability surface---as a zero-shot detection signal.
14	\citet{fast_detectgpt2024} improve computational efficiency by replacing random perturbations with conditional probability curvature from a surrogate model.
15	Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits the perplexity ratio between two related models, achieving strong detection without training data.
16	DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity patterns, while GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} provides statistical visualization of per-token likelihood ranks for human inspection.
17	\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} expose fundamental limits: paraphrasing attacks reduce detection accuracy to near chance, and \citet{pudasaini2026_detection_fails} show detection degrades under distribution shift between training and deployment domains.
18	\citet{pu2026_generator_barrier} formalize a generator barrier bounding detection performance when the generator is unknown.
19	Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster} trains classifiers on statistical features (token probabilities, rank sequences) for binary detection, sharing our feature-engineering philosophy but not addressing depth.
20	The M4-SemEval shared task \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval} benchmarks multilingual machine-generated text detection across diverse generators, and DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt} uses divergent $n$-gram analysis to detect AI text without model access.
21	All these methods perform binary classification (human vs.\ machine), discarding the ordinal depth information that distinguishes first-generation from deeply recursive text.
22	Our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.
23	
24	\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
25	EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the \emph{extent} of editing applied to a passage---a continuous measure of how much a text has been modified in a single pass---but does not model recursive generation chains.
26	\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} formulate authorship attribution as multi-source classification, identifying \emph{which} model generated a text rather than \emph{how many} recursive steps it has undergone.
27	LOKI \cite{loki2025} provides a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple synthetic data modalities but evaluates binary detection, not depth estimation.
28	\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, quantifying information distortion across rounds; while their work measures forward degradation fidelity, our task performs the inverse: classifying generation depth from text alone, without access to the generation chain.
29	
30	\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
31	The choice of decoding strategy shapes the statistical properties of generated text in ways that interact with generation depth signals.
32	\citet{holtzman2020_nucleus} show that unrestricted sampling produces degenerate repetitions and propose nucleus sampling to maintain output diversity.
33	\citet{finlayson2024_closing} demonstrate that decoding parameters affect downstream evaluation metrics in non-trivial ways.
34	\citet{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded} find that the effect of decoding strategies on text quality is model-dependent, complicating universal quality claims.
35	\citet{wiher2022_decoding} provide a systematic comparison of decoding methods on surface-level text properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} introduces perplexity-controlled decoding that actively regulates output entropy.
36	Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects that go beyond single-pass text quality to shape the discriminability of generation depth itself.
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Generalization and Robustness}\n\\label{sec:generalization}\n\nWe test whether the atlas results (69.6--85.4\\%) reflect genuine statistical regularities or training artifacts, evaluating four axes: classifier choice (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:baselines}), cross-model transfer (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossmodel}), cross-strategy transfer (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}), and end-to-end learning (\\S\\ref{sec:gen:e2e}).\n\n\\subsection{Baseline Comparison}\n\\label{sec:gen:baselines}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:baselines} compares classification methods on the Pythia-1.4B nucleus setting.\nThree feature-based methods---Random Forest (RF), CORAL ordinal regression \\cite{coral2020}, and DivEye \\cite{diveye2026}---all operate on the same 19 statistical features and achieve statistically indistinguishable accuracy (78.1--78.2\\%; pairwise bootstrap $p>0.05$ after Bonferroni correction, 95\\% CI within $\\pm$1.1pp).\nThese three significantly outperform CE-MLP ($p<0.001$, $+$3.8pp), which in turn trails logistic regression by $\\sim$0.1pp.\nSingle-feature regression on mean perplexity performs at chance (25.1\\%), confirming that depth estimation requires the multi-dimensional feature representation defined in \\S\\ref{sec:method}.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Comparison of classification methods on Pythia-1.4B nucleus. Train on 2 model families, test on held-out 3rd. Chance = 25\\%. d0 recall $>$98\\% inflates headline accuracy; d1--d3 balanced accuracy averages 55.5\\%.}\n\\label{tab:cross_model}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccccc}\n\\toprule\nHoldout & Acc & d0 & d1 & d2 & d3 \\\\\n & (\\%) & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. \\\\\n\\midrule\nPythia & 62.4 & 100.0 & 49.3 & 26.8 & 73.6 \\\\\nOLMo & \\textbf{69.2} & 99.3 & 75.5 & 43.3 & 58.8 \\\\\nGPT-2 XL & 67.6 & 98.5 & 74.7 & 52.6 & 44.5 \\\\\n\\midrule\nMean & 66.4 & 99.3 & 66.5 & 40.9 & 59.0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nMean transfer accuracy reaches 66.4\\% (2.7$\\times$ chance); d0 recall ($>$98\\%) inflates the headline while d2 drops to 26.8\\% (Pythia holdout).\nExcluding d0, the d1--d3 balanced accuracy averages 55.5\\% across holdout conditions (Pythia 49.9\\%, OLMo 59.2\\%, GPT-2~XL 57.3\\%; chance = 33\\%).\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Strategy Transfer}\n\\label{sec:gen:crossstrategy}\n\nWe train on two decoding strategies and test on the held-out third (Table~\\ref{tab:cross_strategy}).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Cross-strategy transfer (leave-one-out).     "originalFile": "\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\subsection{Problem Definition}\n\\label{sec:method:problem}\n\nLet $f_\\theta$ denote a language model and $\\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.\nWe define a \\emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\\mathcal{D}_0, \\mathcal{D}_1, \\dots, \\mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \\geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\\theta$ on $\\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.\nDepth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \\geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.\n\nGiven a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \\in \\{0, 1, \\dots, K\\}$.\nThis is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.\n\n\\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}\n\\label{sec:method:benchmark}\n\nWe construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.\n\n\\paragraph{Model families.}\nWe select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).\nRestricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.\n\n\\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}\nEach model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \\cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).\nThese span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.\n\n\\paragraph{Depth and scale.}\nThe primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \\times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).\nFor depth extension experiments (\\S\\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.\n\n\\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}\nStarting from a Wikipedia subset as seed text ($\\mathcal{D}_0$), each generation cycle proceeds in three steps: (1)~LoRA finetuning \\cite{hu2022lora} with rank $r{=}16$, $\\alpha{=}32$, learning rate $2{\\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, for 3 epochs; (2)~generation of 5{,}000 passages (max 512 tokens) under the specified decoding strategy; (3)~the generated corpus becomes $\\mathcal{D}_k$ and serves as training data for the next cycle.\nEach generation cycle samples unconditionally from the BOS token; there is no per-passage lineage across depths, ensuring that cross-validation splits do not introduce information leakage.\nLoRA targets are architecture-specific: \\texttt{query\\_key\\_value} for Pythia (GPT-NeoX), \\texttt{q\\_proj}/\\texttt{k\\_proj}/\\texttt{v\\_proj} for OLMo, and \\texttt{c\\_attn}/\\texttt{c\\_proj} for GPT-2~XL.\nWe adopt commonly used LoRA hyperparameters ($r{=}16$, $\\alpha{=}32$, dropout$\\,{=}\\,0.05$) following \\citet{hu2022lora}, applied uniformly across all models.\n\n\\paragraph{Reference model.}\nAll statistical features (\\S\\ref{sec:method:features}) are computed using a fixed reference model---GPT-2 base (124M)---that is independent of the three generation models.\nThe reference model computes per-token perplexity for each passage, providing a consistent measurement frame across model families.\nIn cross-model leave-one-out evaluation (\\S\\ref{sec:generalization}), the reference model remains fixed even when GPT-2~XL is held out; the partial architectural overlap this introduces is discussed in Limitations.\n\n\\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}\n\\label{sec:method:features}\n\nWe extract a 19-dimensional feature vector $\\mathbf{f}(x)$ from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$.\nThe features fall into four categories (Table~\\ref{tab:features}).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).}\n\\label{tab:features}\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}\n\\toprule\nCategory & Features & $n$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nPerplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\\\\nstatistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\\\\n\\addlinespace\nSurprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\\\\nstatistics & & \\\\\n\\addlinespace\nLexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\\\\ndiversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\\\\n\\addlinespace\nRepetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the location, spread, and shape of the per-token perplexity distribution via its mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, and five percentile quantiles (p10--p90).\nThe tail quantiles (p75, p90) prove especially informative: recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail, making these features monotonically decreasing with depth (\\S\\ref{sec:atlas}).\n\n\\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features) operate on $-\\log p(\\text{token})$ and include mean surprisal, surprisal variance, and the entropy of the surprisal distribution.\nWhile correlated with perplexity features, surprisal variance captures second-order structure---the variability of token predictability---that is not redundant with perplexity moments.\n\n\\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features) measures vocabulary usage through type--token ratio, hapax ratio (fraction of tokens appearing exactly once), and bigram/trigram entropy.\n\n\\emph{Repetition} (3 features) quantifies the fraction of repeated $n$-grams for $n \\in \\{2, 3, 4\\}$, capturing the increased self-repetition characteristic of recursive generation.\n\n\\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}\n\\label{sec:method:edd}\n\nAggregate classification accuracy over $K{+}1$ classes obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depths.\nWe introduce the \\emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD), a scalar metric that summarizes how far into a recursive chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.\n\nFor each adjacent depth pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we train a dedicated binary Random Forest (500 trees; increased from 200 in the multi-class setting to ensure convergence on the smaller per-pair samples) and compute the one-vs-one AUC.\nGiven a threshold $T$, we define:\n\\begin{equation}\n\\mathrm{EDD}_T = \\max \\bigl\\{ d^*{+}1 : \\forall\\, d' \\leq d^*,\\; \\mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \\geq T \\bigr\\}\n\\label{eq:edd}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d^* \\in \\{0, 1, \\dots, K{-}1\\}$.\\footnote{Our AUC profiles are monotonically decreasing, so the $\\forall$ and pointwise $\\max\\{d^*{+}1 : \\mathrm{AUC}(d^*,d^*{+}1) \\geq T\\}$ formulations coincide; the $\\forall$ version is preferred as it guarantees a contiguous discriminable range (see Limitations).}\nThe default threshold is $T{=}0.75$; we report sensitivity analyses at $T \\in \\{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\\}$ in \\S\\ref{sec:atlas}.\nCrucially, each AUC is obtained from an independent binary pairwise classifier (5-fold stratified CV) rather than extracted from a single multi-class model, avoiding decision boundary dilution (\\S\\ref{sec:atlas}).\n\nEDD captures a natural question: \\emph{how deep into the recursive chain can we reliably distinguish successive generations?}\nA high EDD indicates that the statistical fingerprints retain discriminative power across many recursion steps; a low EDD signals rapid convergence to an indistinguishable regime.\n\n\\paragraph{Classifiers.}\nOur primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold stratified cross-validation).\nWe compare against CORAL ordinal regression \\cite{coral2020}, DivEye \\cite{diveye2026}, a 2-layer cross-entropy MLP, logistic regression, and a single-feature baseline using mean perplexity alone; results
```
